# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits under the title with the deciding number beside it (Frequency: median 3.5 days out of 7), and 'the verdict is the worst of all its cards' ties the two together.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows who was counted and the bar ('7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7'), but the Frequency card stacks '3 at or beyond, 3 short', '3 of 6 below', 'bar 4 of 6' and '1 short' so that I had to reread it, and the kicker's '6 TO 7 COUNTED' does not say who was left out or why.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are my checked lines word for word, and Prevalence and Frequency carry my own 8-in-10 and 4-to-7-days numbers.
screens.why_b4: The page never says what the split on Frequency means for AirCaps, for example whether to aim the wedge at people who sit at tables every day or to restate the belief as 2 to 3 days a week, so I am left to work it out myself.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, but nothing says that 6 or 7 people is a small sample before 'Holding up' backs 'at least 8 in 10 deaf or hard-of-hearing adults', and the statement's '20% at best' comes from my co-founder's own account and is presented as though the study found it.
screens.instead: Say: 'Split on how often: 3 of 6 lose the thread 4 or more days a week and 3 fewer, one short of your bar. With only 7 answers, either narrow the segment to people in daily group settings or restate it as 2 to 3 days, then send it to more people before building on Frequency.'

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6 of 7, so I know it held and why.
screens.why_b2: The strip counts the people who said yes, over 7, with my bar marked at 6 of 7 (at least 8 in 10), all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Lost the thread of a conversation with hearing people' is recognisably my problem, but the line is Keel's wording of a prevalence belief I don't see among the beliefs I checked on the way in, not my own 'too fast or too noisy to follow'.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' plus a pointer to the next two cards is a generic hand-off; it doesn't tell me what a unanimous yes means for the glasses, such as whether I can stop worrying about whether the problem exists and focus on frequency and severity.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible at 7 and the count line says plainly it is a small group, a lean, not a call, so 7 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: Holding up: all 7 lost the thread at least once this week, so the problem is there; what matters now is whether it happens often enough, and hurts enough, to wear glasses for it. See the next two cards.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits right beside the number that decides it: 3 of 6 at 4 days or more against a bar of 4 of 6, one short, with the median of 3.5 days.
screens.why_b2: What is counted (days out of 7, one cell a person, 6 counted) is plain, but the strip's "marker at 4" means 4 people while the axis below runs 0 to 7 days, so I had to look twice to tell the bar from day 4; the axis also starts at 0, an answer nobody could give.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Frequency and the line "lose the thread of a conversation with hearing people on 4 to 7 days out of 7" is my range and my event, said in my customers' plain words.
screens.why_b4: "Whether it matters is the next card" passes me along without saying what a 3.5-day median means for me, such as whether to aim at the heavier, group-heavy users or to treat 2 to 3 days a week as the real rhythm.
screens.why_b5: The n is shown and the card says "a lean, not a call", but the stray "— the most recent time it happened" after a question that counts days in a week makes me doubt what people were actually asked.
screens.instead: Half of you lose the thread on 4 or more days a week, and the middle answer is 3.5. The pain is real but closer to every other day than daily, so target the people in group-heavy weeks, or test 2 to 3 days as your floor.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 6 put it in their two and bar 4 of 6, so I know it held and by how much over the bar.
screens.why_b2: The caption says 6 people, each picked two, bars count picks (12), my row is marked with 6, and the strip shows 6 cells against a marker at 4, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Importance and carries my belief word for word, five things and all, with my own item Following and joining a conversation named as the problem I named.
screens.why_b4: The So line explains how to read the result (top two, not first) but never says what it means for AirCaps, for example that importance is settled among these six and the open question is how often it happens, which the Frequency card left split.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 6 counted, Tomás set aside as a guess), the small group is called a lean, not a call, and the So line limits itself to these 6 and to top two rather than first.
screens.instead: Say what to do with it: every one of the 6 counted put following the conversation in their two, so importance is not where the problem is in doubt; how often it happens (the split Frequency card) is the belief to test next.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 6 said today's way falls short · bar 4 of 6', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: Each of my five rungs shows its count, the line sits under 'Missed a little, caught up quickly', and the strip of six cells with the marker at 4 shows what is counted, over how many people, and where the bar is.
screens.why_b3: The title is Current solution and the belief line matches word for word what I checked, with my bar's rung quoted exactly, though 'You said' is a stretch since Keel set that bar.
screens.why_b4: It names the gap concretely: three caught the gist and missed details, three lost the thread and nodded along, and nobody followed well. It also says my solution is measured against that gap on the next study, which tells me to pitch the glasses at the detail-missing and nodding-along cases.
screens.why_b5: It keeps the n visible (7 answered, 6 counted), says why Tomás was left out, scopes the claim to 'these 6', and calls it 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so it overclaims nothing.
screens.instead: Say plainly that Keel set the bar rather than 'You said', and tie Tomás's uncounted end-seat quote to the rungs above the line so I see that one partial-hearing case is handled fine today.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Holding up' with '6 of 6 said today's way falls short · bar 4 of 6' right under it, so I know Current solution held and by what count, though the screen's 'When a line fails' heading sits oddly over a line that held.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is named Current solution and the belief about hearing aids or phone captions falling short is word for word the one I checked.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what a held Current solution, or Tomás's workaround, means for AirCaps, and Importance, which also held, gets no box or note at all, so I'm left to work out the next step myself.
screens.why_b5: The quote is fairly marked 'not counted, with no recent time behind them', but the 'When a line fails' heading over a held line and the dangling 'Missed a little, caught up quickly / not counted' fragment read as if something failed when it did not.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's end-seat trick, keeping everyone on his good side, is something I did not type: it shows that people deaf in one ear can often manage today, which is a soft spot in my wedge worth probing.
screens.instead: Current solution held, 6 of 6 (bar 4 of 6); the one person whose way works is deaf on one side and manages by seating, so check whether single-sided hearing loss belongs in the segment; Importance also held, 6 of 6, with no why asked.

screens.why1: As the first question it obviously checks that I'm someone who deals with hearing people regularly, which is what a study like this would need to know before anything else.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is my own everyday word, but 'talk' left me wondering whether signing through an interpreter or texting a hearing coworker counts, or only face-to-face speech and lipreading.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I deal with hearing people every week: at work, the shops, the doctor's.
screens.why4: A yes-or-no screener has a complete, distinct pair, and no escape is expected on a gate.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the founder's plan reaches me, and 'hearing people' is how I'd say it myself.
screens.why6: It is short, one question and two options, easy to take in at once, though for me it would need to be on screen or captioned as well as spoken.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you have a face-to-face conversation with hearing people, in person rather than by text? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking if I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether one of those conversations got away from me in the last week.
screens.why2: "Lose the thread" is exactly how I'd say it: everyone's laughing and I've no idea what about anymore.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether that happened to me this week, at the shop counter, at work, or round someone's kitchen table.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly, and the two chips are for the story box after a Yes, not extra answers to this question.
screens.why5: Nothing here hints at any product or gadget; it only asks about my own conversations.
screens.why6: One short question with the week and the thing that went wrong, then "Yes or no", easy to take in at once.
screens.why7: The gate names the 7-day window and the costly thing, losing the thread, rather than just talking with hearing people, so someone with a good week or good aids can truly say No and I can truly say Yes, and there are two fixed answers with no escape.

screens.why1: I just said yes to losing the thread in the last week, so asking how many days it happened follows naturally.
screens.why2: Losing the thread is exactly how I'd put it, and 'how many days' in the last 7 is clear the first time I hear or read it.
screens.why3: I know which days I had a hard time at the shop counter, at work or at dinner, so I can count them from my own week.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7 covers every true answer, there's no 0 because I already said yes, and 'I can't recall' is a fair way out.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, a device or captions reaches me; it's only about my own conversations.
screens.why6: It's one short question, 'say a number from 1 to 7' is easy to hold, and the escape is said once at the end.
screens.why7: It's on one measure (days out of the 7), runs 1 to 7 in order with no 0 and no bands, counts days rather than times, uses an event that happens on a given day, and has 'I can't recall' as the only escape; the buttons can fall on either side of the founder's low, so the belief can be supported or refuted.

screens.why1: After asking how often I lost the thread, it makes sense to ask which of the hard parts I'd most want eased.
screens.why2: Every option is in words I'd use myself about getting by with hearing people, and I could answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: These are all things I deal with week to week, so I can answer from my own last week.
screens.why4: 'Following and joining a conversation' already holds 'getting a word in at the right moment', so the two overlap, and 'not being worn out by listening' reads as a feeling rather than a thing I do.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, a device or the company's own terms reaches me; it's just the parts of talking with hearing people.
screens.why6: One short question and five short options read as a list, with the escape last, so I could hold it on one hearing.
screens.why7: The own item is there, not first, and 'None of these' is at the first ask, so the belief can go either way; but the own row is the whole job and swallows 'getting a word in', and two rivals drift off face-to-face talk to announcements and phone or video calls.
screens.instead: Think of your last week of talking with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Following a conversation that's fast or noisy · Getting a word in at the right moment · Keeping up when several people talk at once · Asking people to repeat without feeling awkward · None of these

screens.why1: After asking how often I lost the thread and what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last conversation actually went is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Following a conversation with hearing aids or phone captions" makes me stop and work out whether it means my hearing aids or the captions, and it repeats "conversation" and drops "with hearing people", so I'd need a second read.
screens.why3: My last conversation is mine to answer, but the stem assumes I used hearing aids or phone captions, and plenty of us lip-read, use an interpreter, ask people to write it down, or use nothing, so some would have to guess which part applies.
screens.why4: The five run cleanly from following nearly everything to not following at all, each is distinct and in words I'd use ("mostly nodded along" is exactly what happens), and "I can't recall" fits an act nobody else can do for me.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product or the founder's terms for me comes through; hearing aids and phone captions are ordinary things in my life, not a pitch.
screens.why6: The options say well as a list of five, but the stem's "following a conversation with hearing aids or phone captions" is a mouthful heard once, with an "or" in the middle of it.
screens.why7: All five rungs grade one measure, how much of the conversation I followed; they run best to worst with working rungs at the top (followed nearly everything, caught up quickly) and outright failure last, so the belief can be both supported and refuted, and the one escape is "I can't recall", the right one for an act that can't be handed off. The method named in the stem is a fault of the stem, scored under R2 and R3, not of the options.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? Followed nearly everything said; missed a little, caught up quickly; caught the gist, missed the details; lost the thread and mostly nodded along; could not follow it at all. Or: I can't recall.
